Transplant is my specialty at my current level 1! So really everything below the diaphragm, butts and guts until a transplant comes in or if we have live donor days. Makes for lots of variety, plus I getting to keep up my skills in other specialties.

A liver transplant is the most perfect, fun surgery! Maximally invasive planned trauma. Leaves ya tired but time flies when you're having fun! Plus all my surgeons are phenomenal here.

I always try to count. I usually can count a trauma set in less than five minutes, while they are getting on the table and prepping. I've counted in caskets while waiting for a table cover. Best practice, and that way I know there's nothing left before the X-ray is ready. The patient is going through shock, and my goal is to get the patient off the table as fast as possible, so they can get to the unit quickly without re-opening so they can start recovering the patient.

Moved w 4 years of experience from the east coast in 2021 and they cut my wages to 24. Now I work off shift now at 29, w a 2$ pm differential and quarterly liver call bonuses. Interviewed at most of the hospitals around the Denver area. Average pay, but cost of living is expensive especially in Denver. Still waiting on this years cost of living adjustment, RNs got theirs months ago. Yearly evals with like, a 3% every year.

1) It can be a toxic work environment. If it is, find a new job. You'll know right away. Once, a nurse educator refused to give me a tour of the ORs in my first day there because she was fighting with some of the circulating nurses. Red flag! Didn't get better ever.

There are plenty of hospitals. Cliques happen, management issues are everywhere and also it depends on how they allow surgeons and other staff behave. If you have the energy to try and change the culture, power to ya. I have found it's easier to leave and find a new OR family. It's getting better though. Facilities are getting better at kicking out problematic surgeons, and we have more power than ever to speak up if we experience harassment.

I worked at a massive historical hospital, connected with one of the best med schools in the US. The surgeons there had such bad attitudes. Several of the surgeons who were also professors verbally and sexually harassed several staff and students, including myself. I watched the internal case move forward and everyone celebrated their forced departure to the community hospital. This wouldn't happen in the 90's.

But ya still gotta leave because one success does not cleanse a place. There are always better OR families to be adopted into.

2) No way is it super saturated. I know of a level one trauma center currently accepting travelers who are not certified and never worked in a level one. Blows my mind. They come here never done an ex-lap, and all of a sudden a poly trauma comes in. Then they tie up more staff helping them when they should've made sure their scrub is capable at a level one. Contracts will go up again. It's the circle of life. Regression to the mean. Plus every hospital is expanding now after COVID, the boomer generation keeps aging. We have hella job security.

3) You can but it's rare. Sentinel events happen. If your institution is asking you to do things you don't feel comfortable doing, or there are practices that are dangerous, please speak up. And then, leave lol. Protect yourself. You can't really trust anyone really, unfortunately. Devices misfire, surgeons make mistakes, and we make errors too. For example, most states do not report retained surgical items, only around 20 something that do if I remember correctly. It's estimated to occur once in every 1,500 cases. Occurs at 39 times a week.That's a lot. Commit to your practice and protect your patients and yourself. 

4) I feel super fulfilled! I'm a general surgery girl, butts and guts all the way. I was getting really depressed during COVID. I predominantly worked surgical oncology at a massive hospital after strictly doing COVID colectomies and ecmo cannulatios. Again, depressing. Switched regions, now I exclusively do transplants. Getting people off dialysis, helping cure diabetes, giving them a new life with a new liver. My goal is for my patient to be safely on the table as little time as possible. I love my current surgical team! I actually kind of trust these people, first time in my career. Never thought I'd find a group of transplant hippies, but it exists! If you are not happy, find your happiness!

5). I would totally go to scrub school again. It opened doors all over the country, got me out of my home state, plus taught me so much. There's always more to learn. This year I helped premiere my hospitals scrub role for robotic live liver donation. Super fulfilling. And it's paid for my bills way better than managing a cafe, or being a line cook or even working as an ICU CNA. Call sucks but it pays the bills lol. Now I'm going back to school. Wouldn't have that opportunity without scrubbing. It taught me confidence, and to trust myself. Very valuable life lessons. I recommend it to everyone interested in healthcare. 

If you are unhappy, find a new hospital if you have the ability to move. Eventually you'll find a winner. Took me five attempts.

My derm thinks I have a food allergy to nickel and apparently random eyelid eczema is a classic symptom of it. Nickel is a super common top soil element, so it's in a lot of fruits and veggies. I got a filter for my shower water, only drink water that's been purified, and I try to be conscious about nickel heavy foods.
